Wilson's theorem. A mathematical principle that states a positive integer p greater than one is prime if and only if the quantity p minus one factorial is congruent to negative one modulo p. This elegant characterization of primes through factorials is named after John Wilson and was rigorously proved by Joseph-Louis Lagrange. It is a beautiful theoretical result, though computationally inefficient for primality testing compared to modern algorithms. The theorem provides an if-and-only-if characterization: p is prime exactly when p minus one factorial is congruent to negative one modulo p. Let me illustrate with an example. For p equals five, we have four factorial equals twenty-four, which is congruent to negative one, or equivalently four, modulo five, so five is prime. The converse also holds: if p is composite and p is greater than four, then p minus one factorial is congruent to zero modulo p, because p divides the factorial. Although theoretically elegant, Wilson's theorem is impractical for primality testing of large numbers because computing p minus one factorial modulo p becomes computationally prohibitive. Computing the factorial of a large number and then reducing it modulo p involves an enormous number of multiplications. The theorem reveals a deep symmetry in modular arithmetic and has inspired generalizations in abstract algebra, connecting primes to the structure of multiplicative groups and finite fields.
